title: Maths & Logic
blurb: Numbers, chance, shapes, statistics and clear thinking.

cards.title: The invention of zero
cards.text: Zero as a number, not just a gap, was developed in India; Brahmagupta wrote rules for it around 628 CE. It reached Europe through Arabic scholars, with Hindu-Arabic numerals.

cards.title: Place value
cards.text: In 352, the 3 means three hundreds because of its place. Roman numerals had no place value, which made arithmetic painful: try CCCLII × XLVII.

cards.title: Pi
cards.text: π is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter: about 3.14159. Its digits never end or repeat. Archimedes estimated it around 250 BCE.

cards.title: Prime numbers
cards.text: A prime has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… Euclid proved around 300 BCE that there are infinitely many.

cards.title: Primes protect your data
cards.text: Multiplying two huge primes is easy; working backwards to find them is extremely hard. RSA encryption, used online, relies on that.

cards.title: The Fibonacci sequence
cards.text: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21… It appears in sunflower seed spirals and pine cones.

cards.title: Square numbers
cards.text: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Odd numbers add up to them: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

cards.title: Infinity
cards.text: Some infinities are bigger than others. Georg Cantor showed there are more real numbers (all decimals) than whole numbers, even though both are infinite.

cards.title: Negative numbers
cards.text: Negative numbers were used in China over 2,000 years ago for debts. Europeans resisted them until the 1600s. Today they're on every thermometer and bank statement.

cards.title: A trick with 9
cards.text: Multiply 9 by any number from 1 to 10 and the digits of the answer add up to 9: 9 × 7 = 63, and 6 + 3 = 9.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prime number?

cards.title: Probability basics
cards.text: Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A fair coin landing heads is 1/2; rolling a six is 1/6.

cards.title: And and or
cards.text: For independent events, multiply for "and": two heads = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Add for "either", if they can't both happen: a 1 or a 2 on a die = 2/6.

cards.title: The gambler's fallacy

items.w: "Red came up 5 times, black is due"
items.r: Each spin is independent: same odds

cards.text: After five heads in a row, tails isn't "due". Coins have no memory; the next flip is still 50/50.

cards.title: The birthday paradox
cards.text: In a group of just 23 people, there's a better than 50% chance two share a birthday. With 70 people, it's over 99.9%.

cards.title: Expected value
cards.text: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add. A lottery ticket costing €2 with an expected payout of €1 loses €1 on average.

cards.title: Lotteries
cards.text: EuroMillions jackpot odds are about 1 in 140 million. You're far more likely to be struck by lightning in your lifetime.

cards.title: The Monty Hall problem
cards.text: Pick one of three doors; the host, who knows, opens a losing door and offers a switch. Switching wins 2/3 of the time. Even mathematicians got it wrong at first.

cards.title: Base rates
cards.text: A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 1,000 people. If you test positive, the chance you have it is only about 9%, because false positives from healthy people outnumber true cases.

cards.title: Law of large numbers
cards.text: Over a few flips, results can be lopsided. Over thousands, the share of heads gets very close to 50%. Casinos rely on this.

cards.title: Risk in perspective
cards.text: "Doubles the risk" sounds scary, but from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 is a tiny absolute change. Always ask: out of how many?

quiz.q: After 5 heads in a row, the next flip is…
In the Monty Hall problem, switching wins…
How many people make a shared birthday more likely than not?

cards.title: Pythagoras' theorem
cards.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the longest side equals the sum of the squares on the other two. Builders used 3-4-5 triangles to make square corners.

cards.title: The 3-4-5 triangle
cards.text: Measure 3 m along one wall and 4 m along the other. If the diagonal is exactly 5 m, the corner is a perfect right angle.

cards.title: Angles in a triangle
cards.text: The angles in any triangle add up to 180°. Those in a four-sided shape add up to 360°.

cards.title: Area of a circle
cards.text: A circle's area is π times the radius squared. Doubling the radius makes the area four times bigger: why a 40 cm pizza is more than one and a half 30 cm pizzas.

cards.title: Hexagons in nature
cards.text: Bees build hexagonal cells because hexagons tile a surface with no gaps using the least wall material for the area enclosed.

cards.title: Platonic solids
cards.text: Only five solids have identical regular faces with the same number meeting at each corner: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. Dice use them.

cards.title: Symmetry
cards.text: A shape has symmetry if a move, such as a reflection or rotation, leaves it looking the same. Snowflakes have six-fold symmetry; your face is roughly mirror-symmetric.

cards.title: Scaling
cards.text: If you double the size of an object, its area grows four times and its volume eight times. That's why giant insects couldn't hold themselves up.

cards.title: Map projections
cards.text: You can't flatten a sphere without distortion. The Mercator map keeps angles right for navigation but makes Greenland look as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.

cards.title: Fractals
cards.text: Fractals repeat their pattern at every scale: coastlines, ferns, broccoli and lightning. Zoom in and you see the same shape again.

quiz.q: What's the hypotenuse of a triangle with sides 3 and 4?
Double the size of a cube: its volume grows…

cards.title: Mean, median, mode
cards.text: The mean is the average; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most common. They can differ a lot.

cards.title: When the mean misleads
cards.text: If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth of the customers shoots up, but the median barely moves. Salaries are better described by the median.

cards.title: Spread
cards.text: Two classes can have the same average but very different spreads. The standard deviation measures how far values typically are from the mean.

cards.title: The bell curve
cards.text: Many measurements, like heights, cluster around an average in a bell shape. About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation and 95% within two.

cards.title: Samples
cards.text: A well-chosen random sample of 1,000 people can represent millions. A big but biased sample can't: who you ask matters more than how many.

cards.title: Margin of error
cards.text: Polls report a margin of error. With about 1,000 people it's roughly ±3 percentage points, so 51% vs 49% may be a tie.

cards.title: Misleading charts

items.r: Check the axis: it's a 2% difference

cards.text: A chart's y-axis that doesn't start at zero can make a small difference look huge. Always check the scale.

cards.title: Simpson's paradox
cards.text: A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined. A treatment can look better in each hospital but worse overall, if hospitals have different patient mixes.

cards.title: Regression to the mean
cards.text: After an extreme result, the next tends to be closer to average. A sports star's record season is often followed by a more ordinary one, without any curse.

cards.title: Reading a news statistic
cards.text: Ask four questions: compared with what? Out of how many? Who was measured? Who paid for the study?

quiz.q: Which average is best for describing typical salaries?
quiz.explain: A few very high earners pull the mean up.

quiz.q: About what share of values fall within 1 standard deviation in a bell curve?

lessons.title: Logic and puzzles
lessons.summary: Clear thinking, from paradoxes to computers.

cards.title: True and false

items.b: true if at least one true

cards.text: Logic works with statements that are true or false and combines them with AND, OR and NOT. Every computer chip is built from these operations.

cards.title: If… then…

items.r: Something else could have wet it

cards.text: "If it rains, the ground is wet" doesn't mean "if the ground is wet, it rained": a sprinkler could do that. Confusing the two is a classic logic error.

cards.title: Proof by contradiction
cards.text: Assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show it leads to nonsense. Euclid proved infinitely many primes this way.

cards.title: The liar paradox
cards.text: "This sentence is false." If it's true, it's false; if it's false, it's true. Paradoxes like this shook the foundations of logic in the 20th century.

cards.title: Gödel's incompleteness
cards.text: In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent system of rules rich enough for arithmetic has true statements it can't prove. Mathematics can never be complete.

cards.title: Algorithms
cards.text: An algorithm is a precise step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. The word comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century mathematician in Baghdad.

cards.title: Binary
cards.text: Computers count in base 2, using only 0 and 1. Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…

cards.title: Zeno's paradox
cards.text: To cross a room, you must first cross half, then half of what's left, forever. Zeno said you'd never arrive. The infinite sum 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … actually equals 1.

cards.title: Unsolved problems
cards.text: Some simple-sounding questions remain unsolved, like Goldbach's conjecture: is every even number above 2 the sum of two primes? Tested to huge numbers, never proved.

cards.title: The river crossing
cards.text: A farmer must cross a river with a wolf, a goat and a cabbage, taking one at a time. The wolf can't be left with the goat, nor the goat with the cabbage. The trick: bring the goat back.

quiz.q: What is 101 in binary as a normal number?
"If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet." Does it follow that it rained?
quiz.explain: Something else could have wet it.
